claim: Rotavirus (RV) is a major causative agent of severe dehydrating diarrhea in children under five years.
source: RV, a major causative agent of severe dehydrating diarrhea in children under five years (GBD Diarrhoeal Diseases Collaborators, 2017), is a multilayered virus of clinical relevance and one of the main study models for the Reoviridae family.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to GBD Diarrhoeal Diseases Collaborators, 2017.

claim: The RV infectious particle is a 100 nm non-enveloped triple-layered particle (TLP) composed of three concentric protein shells enclosing the dsRNA genome and the viral RNA polymerase and capping enzyme.
source: The RV infectious particle is a 100 nm non-enveloped triple-layered particle (TLP) composed of three concentric protein shells enclosing the dsRNA genome and the viral RNA polymerase and capping enzyme (Figure 1A) (Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Settembre et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The inner layer is a T = 1 capsid formed by 60 asymmetric dimers of the VP2 protein (102 kDa).
source: The inner layer is a T = 1 capsid formed by 60 asymmetric dimers of the VP2 protein (102 kDa) that surrounds the eleven dsRNA genomic segments associated with the RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase VP1 (125 kDa) and the RNA-capping enzyme VP3 (88 kDa) at the pentameric positions (Estrozi et al., 2013; Periz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Estrozi et al., 2013 and Periz et al., 2013.

claim: The single-layered particle (SLP) is surrounded by a thick T = 13 layer formed by 260 VP6 pear-shaped trimers (45 kDa) in the double-layered particle (DLP).
source: This thin single-layered particle (SLP), an intermediate structure that is involved in the packing and replication of the viral genome, is surrounded by a thick T = 13 layer formed by 260 VP6 pear-shaped trimers (45 kDa) (Settembre et al., 2011; McClain et al., 2010) in the double-layered particle (DLP).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Settembre et al., 2011 and McClain et al., 2010.

claim: The DLP does not disassemble during the infection and constitutes the transcriptional machinery that initiates the core steps of the viral replication cycle once delivered in the host cell cytoplasm.
source: This particle, which does not disassemble during the infection, constitutes the transcriptional machinery that initiates the core steps of the viral replication cycle once delivered in the host cell cytoplasm (Cohen et al., 1979; Bass et al., 1992; Lawton et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 1979; Bass et al., 1992; Lawton et al., 1997.

claim: The DLP is not infectious since it cannot recognize, bind to and penetrate the host target cell.
source: The DLP is not infectious since it cannot recognize, bind to and penetrate the host target cell.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about DLP properties.

claim: The VP7 glycoprotein is organized as 260 Ca2+-stabilized trimers that cap and embrace through its N-terminal arm each VP6 trimer of the DLP.
source: The VP7 glycoprotein is organized as 260 Ca2+-stabilized trimers that cap and embrace through its N-terminal arm each VP6 trimer of the DLP (Settembre et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Settembre et al., 2011 and Chen et al., 2009.

claim: The viral spike must be proteolytically processed to VP5* and VP8* by trypsin-like proteases from the intestinal lumen or from within cells to generate a fully-infectious virion.
source: The viral spike is formed by three copies of VP4 that must be proteolytically processed to VP5* and VP8* by trypsin-like proteases from the intestinal lumen or from within cells to generate a fully-infectious virion (Settembre et al., 2011; Estes et al., 1979; Estes et al., 1981; Clark et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Settembre et al., 2011; Estes et al., 1979; Estes et al., 1981; Clark et al., 1981.

claim: The assembly of the VP6 T = 13 layer on the 60 VP2 dimers (T = 1) that build the SLP is one of the best examples of symmetry mismatch.
source: Interestingly, the assembly of the VP6 T = 13 layer on the 60 VP2 dimers (T = 1) that build the SLP is one of the best examples of symmetry mismatch, of which the consequences for virus particle stability are still not well understood.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation about the structural arrangement.

claim: The symmetry mismatch between VP6 and VP2 layers is preserved in most reoviruses and has been associated with the regulation of the polymerase activity.
source: This mismatch is preserved in most reoviruses, and has been associated with the regulation of the polymerase activity (McClain et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McClain et al., 2010.

claim: AFM directly probed the existence of pressure in some phages that is used to translocate their genome into the host.
source: AFM directly probed the existence of pressure (Kindt et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2001) in some phages (Evilevitch et al., 2011; Hernando-Pérez et al., 2012) that is used to translocate their genome into the host (González-Huici et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kindt et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2001; Evilevitch et al., 2011; Hernando-Pérez et al., 2012; González-Huici et al., 2004.

claim: Human adenovirus pressurizes during maturation, and this pressure is related to the degree of condensation of the dsDNA of the viral minichromosome.
source: In a similar way, it has been found that human adenovirus pressurizes during maturation, and that this pressure is related to the degree of condensation of the dsDNA of the viral minichromosome (Ortega-Esteban et al., 2015a; Ortega-Esteban et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ortega-Esteban et al., 2015a and Ortega-Esteban et al., 2015b.

claim: RV TLP can be converted to DLP by disassembling the outer VP4-VP7 layer with chelating agents such as ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).
source: Previous studies have shown that RV TLP can be converted to DLP by disassembling the outer VP4-VP7 layer with chelating agents such as ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (Estes et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Estes et al., 1979.

claim: DLP can be converted to SLP by chaotropic agents such as CaCl2.
source: Once purified, DLP can be converted to SLP by chaotropic agents such as CaCl2 (Figure 1B) (Bican et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bican et al., 1982 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Homogeneous populations of TLP, DLP and SLP were obtained, as indicated by SDS-PAGE and negative staining electron microscopy analysis.
source: Homogeneous populations of TLP, DLP and SLP were obtained, as indicated by SDS-PAGE and negative staining electron microscopy analysis (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C-E showing experimental results.

claim: Spike polypeptides (VP5*/VP8*) and VP7 glycoprotein are totally removed in purified DLP.
source: Spike polypeptides (VP5*/VP8*) and VP7 glycoprotein are totally removed in purified DLP (Figure 1D) while VP6 is absent in the isolated cores (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing experimental results.

claim: VP6 is absent in the isolated cores (SLP).
source: Spike polypeptides (VP5*/VP8*) and VP7 glycoprotein are totally removed in purified DLP (Figure 1D) while VP6 is absent in the isolated cores (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1E showing experimental results.

claim: High resolution AFM images are compatible with the structures obtained from cryo-EM and x-ray, where thousands and millions of particles are averaged, respectively.
source: Our high resolution images (Figure 2) are compatible with the structures obtained from cryo-EM (Settembre et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2008) and x-ray (McClain et al., 2010), where thousands and millions of particles are averaged, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Settembre et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2008; McClain et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Spikes protruding from the TLP as well as the DLP pentameric and hexameric depressions are resolved in AFM images.
source: Spikes protruding from the TLP (Figure 2A) as well as the DLP pentameric and hexameric depressions (Figure 2B) are resolved.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A and 2B showing AFM images.

claim: SLP offers featureless structure in AFM images.
source: In contrast, SLP offers featureless structure (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2C showing AFM images.

claim: TLP exhibit a broad distribution of height values.
source: Although the distinctive topography of TLP allows their unambiguous identification, they exhibit a broad distribution of height values (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D-E showing height measurements.

claim: The broad distribution of TLP height values is probably due to the number of spikes present at the interface between the particles and the substrate surface and to the mode of how they influence the particle adsorption.
source: This behavior is probably due to the number of spikes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) present at the interface between the particles and the substrate surface and to the mode of how they influence the particle adsorption.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed height distribution data.

claim: The height data of TLP suggest two populations centered at ~74 and ~62 nm.
source: The height data of TLP (Figure 2E, red) suggest two populations centered at ~74 and ~62 nm, represented by filled and empty symbols, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E showing height measurements.

claim: The two TLP height populations correspond to the presence or absence of spikes at the particle-surface interface.
source: We propose that these data correspond to the presence (red filled squares, Figure 2E) or absence (red empty squares, Figure 2E) of spikes at the particle-surface interface.
evidence: The claim is a proposed interpretation of the height data.

claim: When spikes are present at the particle-surface interface, they prevent partially the contact between the VP7 layer and the substrate, thus precluding virus adsorption and deformation.
source: In the first case the presence of spikes would prevent partially the contact between the VP7 layer and the substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), thus precluding virus adsorption and deformation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the VP7 layer directly rests on the surface, TLP collapse to an average height value of 62 nm probably due to a strong VP7-surface interaction.
source: However, when the VP7 layer directly rests on the surface, TLP collapse to an average height value of 62 nm (Figure 2) probably due to a strong VP7-surface interaction (Zeng et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 2 and citation to Zeng et al., 2017a.

claim: DLP and SLP present a narrower height distribution than TLP.
source: In contrast, DLP and SLP present a narrower height distribution (Figure 2E) whose average values are compatible with the nominal values (70 nm for DLP and 55 nm for SLP), indicating a little deformation due to the adsorption on the surface of 6% and 2% for DLP and SLP respectively (Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E and citations to Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b.

claim: The average height values of DLP and SLP are compatible with the nominal values (70 nm for DLP and 55 nm for SLP).
source: In contrast, DLP and SLP present a narrower height distribution (Figure 2E) whose average values are compatible with the nominal values (70 nm for DLP and 55 nm for SLP), indicating a little deformation due to the adsorption on the surface of 6% and 2% for DLP and SLP respectively (Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E and citations to Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b.

claim: DLP undergoes 6% deformation due to adsorption on the surface.
source: In contrast, DLP and SLP present a narrower height distribution (Figure 2E) whose average values are compatible with the nominal values (70 nm for DLP and 55 nm for SLP), indicating a little deformation due to the adsorption on the surface of 6% and 2% for DLP and SLP respectively (Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E and citations to Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b.

claim: SLP undergoes 2% deformation due to adsorption on the surface.
source: In contrast, DLP and SLP present a narrower height distribution (Figure 2E) whose average values are compatible with the nominal values (70 nm for DLP and 55 nm for SLP), indicating a little deformation due to the adsorption on the surface of 6% and 2% for DLP and SLP respectively (Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E and citations to Llauró et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2017b.

claim: Icosahedral symmetry imposition renders an ideal RV particle with 60 trimeric spikes.
source: Although icosahedral symmetry imposition renders an ideal RV particle with 60 trimeric spikes (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), previous studies have shown that some positions are unoccupied in the purified TLP (Chen and Ramig, 1992; Trask and Dormitzer, 2006; Rodríguez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citations to Chen and Ramig, 1992; Trask and Dormitzer, 2006; Rodríguez et al., 2014.

claim: Previous studies have shown that some spike positions are unoccupied in the purified TLP.
source: Although icosahedral symmetry imposition renders an ideal RV particle with 60 trimeric spikes (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), previous studies have shown that some positions are unoccupied in the purified TLP (Chen and Ramig, 1992; Trask and Dormitzer, 2006; Rodríguez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Ramig, 1992; Trask and Dormitzer, 2006; Rodríguez et al., 2014.

claim: Densitometric analysis of Coomassie-stained gels produced a spike occupancy of 52%.
source: Densitometric analysis of Coomassie-stained gels (Figure 1C) produced an occupancy of 52%.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing experimental results.

claim: Cryo-EM analysis and three-dimensional reconstruction of TLP showed an equivalent spike occupancy (~50%).
source: Cryo-EM analysis and three-dimensional reconstruction (3DR) of these TLP showed an equivalent occupancy (~50%) when the relative density of the spikes in the 3DR is determined using the VP2-VP6-VP7 shell density as a reference (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing cryo-EM results.

claim: Lateral spikes are easily removed by the AFM tip.
source: Since lateral spikes are easily removed by the AFM tip (Video 1), we analyzed the upper ~1/3 region of the virus surface, where the spikes point upwards and present a maximum resistance to AFM imaging.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Video 1 showing experimental observations.

claim: AFM topographies provide an average spike occupancy of 35%.
source: Our AFM topographies, which uniquely allow for the first time the direct imaging of the individual spikes, provide a more realistic view of the RV virion as a distribution ranging from fully decorated to almost naked particles. (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1). We can directly observe an average occupancy of 35%, compatible with electrophoretic and cryo-EM bulk analysis results.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing AFM measurements.

claim: An occupancy as low as 10% is enough to generate particles with high specific infectivity.
source: These data support the in vitro recoating assays, demonstrating that an occupancy as low as 10% is enough to generate particles with high specific infectivity (Trask and Dormitzer, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trask and Dormitzer, 2006.

claim: TLP breaks into large fragments during nanoindentation.
source: While TLP breaks into large fragments (Figure 3A, right), both DLP and SLP show circular deformations that can be attributed to the tip apex (Figure 3B–C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A showing experimental results.

claim: Both DLP and SLP show circular deformations that can be attributed to the tip apex during nanoindentation.
source: While TLP breaks into large fragments (Figure 3A, right), both DLP and SLP show circular deformations that can be attributed to the tip apex (Figure 3B–C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3B-C showing experimental results.

claim: The average TLP nanoindentation curve shows a linear regime that corresponds to the virus elastic deformation up to ~2.0 nm at ~2.1 nN, where the elastic limit is reached.
source: The average of TLP nanoindentation curves (Figure 3D, strong red) shows a linear regime that corresponds to the virus elastic deformation up to ~2.0 nm at ~2.1 nN, where the elastic limit is reached.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing experimental results.

claim: TLP yields plastically without breaking until 2.5 nN at 4.7 nm, during 2.7 nm.
source: Afterwards the structure yields plastically without breaking until 2.5 nN at 4.7 nm, during 2.7 nm (red double headed arrow, Figure 3D), where the downwards slope indicates fracture.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing experimental results.

claim: DLP undergoes plastic deformation of ~13 nm during nanoindentation.
source: The same reasoning applied to both DLP and SLP result in plastic deformations of ~13 nm and ~39 nm, respectively (blue and green double headed arrows, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing experimental results.

claim: SLP undergoes plastic deformation of ~39 nm during nanoindentation.
source: The same reasoning applied to both DLP and SLP result in plastic deformations of ~13 nm and ~39 nm, respectively (blue and green double headed arrows, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing experimental results.

claim: TLP undergoes a brittle (glass-like) fracture.
source: Virus topographies and indentation assays indicate that while TLP undergoes a brittle (glass-like) fracture, both DLP and SLP experience ductile (rubber-like) breakage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the topography and indentation data.

claim: Both DLP and SLP experience ductile (rubber-like) breakage.
source: Virus topographies and indentation assays indicate that while TLP undergoes a brittle (glass-like) fracture, both DLP and SLP experience ductile (rubber-like) breakage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the topography and indentation data.

claim: The spring constant of TLP is kTLP = 0.76 ± 0.30 N/m.
source: Statistical analysis of the FIC linear part result in spring constants of kTLP = 0.76 ± 0.30 N/m, kDLP = 0.34 ± 0.20 N/m and kSLP = 0.22 ± 0.07 N/m.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of force-indentation curves.

claim: The spring constant of DLP is kDLP = 0.34 ± 0.20 N/m.
source: Statistical analysis of the FIC linear part result in spring constants of kTLP = 0.76 ± 0.30 N/m, kDLP = 0.34 ± 0.20 N/m and kSLP = 0.22 ± 0.07 N/m.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of force-indentation curves.

claim: The spring constant of SLP is kSLP = 0.22 ± 0.07 N/m.
source: Statistical analysis of the FIC linear part result in spring constants of kTLP = 0.76 ± 0.30 N/m, kDLP = 0.34 ± 0.20 N/m and kSLP = 0.22 ± 0.07 N/m.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of force-indentation curves.

claim: The breaking force of TLP is 2.9 ± 0.5 nN.
source: The analysis of the breaking force provides values of 2.9 ± 0.5 nN, 0.9 ± 0.3 nN and 0.45 ± 0.10 nN for TLP, DLP and SLP, respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B showing experimental results.

claim: The breaking force of DLP is 0.9 ± 0.3 nN.
source: The analysis of the breaking force provides values of 2.9 ± 0.5 nN, 0.9 ± 0.3 nN and 0.45 ± 0.10 nN for TLP, DLP and SLP, respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B showing experimental results.

claim: The breaking force of SLP is 0.45 ± 0.10 nN.
source: The analysis of the breaking force provides values of 2.9 ± 0.5 nN, 0.9 ± 0.3 nN and 0.45 ± 0.10 nN for TLP, DLP and SLP, respectively (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B showing experimental results.

claim: The monotonic decrease of both the spring constant and breaking force with the reduction of the number of layers indicates that virus mechanics captures the reinforcement nature of concentric shells.
source: This monotonic decrease of both the spring constant and breaking force with the reduction of the number of layers indicates that virus mechanics captures the reinforcement nature of concentric shells: the more layers in the structure, the stronger it becomes.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the mechanical measurements.

claim: The simultaneous high rigidity and yield strain of TLP is exceptional since an increment in the spring constant and breaking force is usually associated with a lower yield strain.
source: This simultaneous high rigidity and yield strain is exceptional since an increment in the spring constant and breaking force is usually associated with a lower yield strain as it happens, for example, with glass (Schijve, 2009).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by a citation to Schijve, 2009.

claim: The relatively low packing fraction of RV (~20%) compared to pressurized dsDNA viruses suggests a small pressure whose influence on the effective elastic constant will be smaller than the error bars.
source: The relatively low packing fraction of RV (~20%) compared to pressurized dsDNA viruses (Purohit et al., 2005) suggests a small pressure whose influence on the effective elastic constant will be smaller than our error bars.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by a citation to Purohit et al., 2005.

claim: The Young's modulus of VP2 layer is YVP2 = 0.53 ± 0.20 GPa.
source: The nanoindentation of SLP was implemented first, yielding a value for the Young's modulus of YVP2 = 0.53 ± 0.20 GPa.
evidence: The claim is supported by finite element simulations of experimental data.

claim: The Young's modulus of VP6 layer is YVP6 = 0.08 ± 0.07 GPa.
source: A second layer of 8 nm thickness, representing that of VP6, was added on top of the VP2 layer, and a Young's modulus YVP6 = 0.08 ± 0.07 GPa was needed to recover the spring constant of DLP, kDLP.
evidence: The claim is supported by finite element simulations of experimental data.

claim: The Young's modulus of VP7 layer is YVP7 = 1.0 ± 0.9 GPa.
source: Finally, a 3.5 nm thick third layer was placed on top of the DLP, requiring a Young's modulus YVP7 = 1.0 ± 0.9 GPa to yield the same spring constant as the TLP, kTLP.
evidence: The claim is supported by finite element simulations of experimental data.

claim: The ratio of Young's modulus between VP7 and VP6 layers is YVP7 / YVP6=12.
source: We can compare the Young's modulus between layers resulting in YVP7 / YVP6=12 and YVP2 / YVP6=6.5.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the Young's modulus values obtained from simulations.

claim: The ratio of Young's modulus between VP2 and VP6 layers is YVP2 / YVP6=6.5.
source: We can compare the Young's modulus between layers resulting in YVP7 / YVP6=12 and YVP2 / YVP6=6.5.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the Young's modulus values obtained from simulations.

claim: The VP7 layer accumulates most of the stress in TLP during nanoindentation.
source: Figure 4C shows the map of the stress supported by the constituent layers of each subviral particle, demonstrating that the VP7 layer accumulates most of the stress in TLP.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4C showing finite element simulation results.

claim: The VP7 shell is the stiffer layer of the RV structure, but also the most elastic.
source: Thus, nanoindentation experiments and FE analysis, indicate the VP7 shell to be the stiffer layer of the RV structure, but also the most elastic, whereas the thick VP6 layer is remarkably soft and brittle.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of nanoindentation experiments and finite element analysis.

claim: The thick VP6 layer is remarkably soft and brittle.
source: Thus, nanoindentation experiments and FE analysis, indicate the VP7 shell to be the stiffer layer of the RV structure, but also the most elastic, whereas the thick VP6 layer is remarkably soft and brittle.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of nanoindentation experiments and finite element analysis.

claim: Cyclic imaging of the TLP at forces between 100 pN to 200 pN per pixel shows that the VP4 spikes are removed from the particle surface in a few frames.
source: Cyclic imaging of the TLP (Figure 5A, left) at forces between 100 pN to 200 pN per pixel shows that, while the VP4 spikes are removed from the particle surface in a few frames (Figure 5A, middle and Video 1), the VP7 layer remains mostly intact (Figure 5A, right) during 80 frames (light red in Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5A and Video 1 showing experimental results.

claim: The VP7 layer remains mostly intact during 80 frames of cyclic imaging at forces between 100 pN to 200 pN per pixel.
source: Cyclic imaging of the TLP (Figure 5A, left) at forces between 100 pN to 200 pN per pixel shows that, while the VP4 spikes are removed from the particle surface in a few frames (Figure 5A, middle and Video 1), the VP7 layer remains mostly intact (Figure 5A, right) during 80 frames (light red in Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5A, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 5 showing experimental results.

claim: The spikes are not strongly anchored.
source: These results illustrate that the spikes are easily removed by the AFM tip and are not strongly anchored.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the fatigue experiment results.

claim: The VP7 layer displays a strong resistance against fatigue, in agreement with the high stiffness and breaking force demonstrated in single indentation assay experiments.
source: However, the VP7 layer displays a strong resistance against fatigue, in agreement with the high stiffness and breaking force demonstrated in single indentation assay experiments.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation connecting fatigue and nanoindentation results.

claim: A strong binding energy between capsomers would not only result in a high resistance of individual proteins against fatigue, but also will contribute to a high breaking force when all capsomers are probed in a single indentation assay experiment.
source: A strong binding energy between capsomers would not only result in a high resistance of individual proteins against fatigue, but also will contribute to a high breaking force when all capsomers are probed in a single indentation assay experiment.
evidence: The claim is a general principle relating binding energy to mechanical properties.

claim: The current model proposes a calcium concentration drop in endosomal compartments during RV entry as the factor that triggers VP7 disassembly and membrane penetration.
source: The current model proposes a calcium concentration drop in endosomal compartments during RV entry as the factor that triggers VP7 disassembly and membrane penetration (Arias et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arias et al., 2015.

claim: Calcium depletion by chelating agents (as EDTA) is used to uncoat TLP to DLP by inducing VP7 trimer dissociation.
source: In fact, calcium depletion by chelating agents (as EDTA) (Estes et al., 1979) is used to uncoat TLP to DLP by inducing VP7 trimer dissociation (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Estes et al., 1979 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: In the presence of EDTA, fatigue induces the neat VP7 detachment from the VP6 subjacent layer even before the spikes are removed.
source: In these conditions, fatigue induces the neat VP7 detachment from the VP6 subjacent layer (indicated by a circle in Figure 5B#19) even before the spikes are removed.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B showing experimental results.

claim: The evolution of the topographic profiles shows abrupt downwards steps very close to the VP7 thickness indicating that TLP particle loses VP7 completely while keeping VP6 in the presence of EDTA.
source: Indeed, the evolution of the topographic profiles (dark red in Figure 5E) show abrupt downwards steps very close to the VP7 thickness (red arrow of Figure 5E) indicating that TLP particle loses VP7 completely while keeping VP6 (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5E and Video 2 showing experimental results.

claim: Ca ions mediate the interaction between VP7 and VP6 layers.
source: These results not only suggest that Ca ions mediate the interaction between VP7 and VP6 layers, but also that the absence of ions weakens the interaction between VP7 subunits.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EDTA fatigue experiment results.

claim: The absence of Ca ions weakens the interaction between VP7 subunits.
source: These results not only suggest that Ca ions mediate the interaction between VP7 and VP6 layers, but also that the absence of ions weakens the interaction between VP7 subunits.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the EDTA fatigue experiment results.

claim: VP6 subunits are neatly removed from VP2 layer during continued fatigue in the presence of EDTA.
source: If fatigue continues, VP6 subunits are neatly removed from VP2 layer (circle in Figure 5B#29).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B showing experimental results.

claim: VP6 shell appears as a weak shell whose interaction with the beneath VP2 layer is not very strong, since it peels off rapidly to reveal the SLP.
source: Therefore, VP6 shell appears as a weak shell whose interaction with the beneath VP2 layer is not very strong, since it peels off rapidly to reveal the SLP.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the fatigue experiment results.

claim: Fatigue induced a clean VP6 disassembly from DLP after less than 10 frames.
source: We found similar results on experiments performed on DLP. Again, fatigue induced a clean VP6 disassembly after less than 10 frames (circle in Figure 5C#8, and Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5C and Video 3 showing experimental results.

claim: The evolution of the topographic profiles of DLP undergoes sharp reductions very close to the VP6 thickness, inducing the gradual uncovering of the innermost VP2.
source: In this case the evolution of the topographic profiles (blue in Figure 5E) undergoes sharp reductions very close to the VP6 thickness, inducing the gradual uncovering of the innermost VP2 (blue arrow in Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5E showing experimental results.

claim: DLP fatigue experiments illustrate a weak interaction between VP6 and VP2 layers.
source: These experiments not only illustrate a weak interaction between VP6 and VP2 layers, but also a very feeble VP6-VP6 binding force.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the DLP fatigue experiment results.

claim: DLP fatigue experiments illustrate a very feeble VP6-VP6 binding force.
source: These experiments not only illustrate a weak interaction between VP6 and VP2 layers, but also a very feeble VP6-VP6 binding force.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the DLP fatigue experiment results.

claim: The thin SLP VP2 is highly unstable under fatigue experiments collapsing well before reaching 10 frames.
source: Finally, the thin SLP VP2 is highly unstable under fatigue experiments collapsing well before reaching 10 frames (green in Figure 5D, and Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5D and Video 4 showing experimental results.

claim: Removing of Ca ions is key for inducing the transition from TLP to DLP in the fatigue experiments.
source: We have seen that removing of Ca ions is key for inducing the transition from TLP to DLP in the fatigue experiments (Figure 5A–B, and red charts in Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 5A-B and Figure 5E.

claim: A controlled FIC on TLP can produce local disruptions in the TLP shell that reach a maximum depth of ~23 nm that includes the thickness of the three layers.
source: Right after the FIC (Figure 6A#25), the induced fracture reaches a maximum depth of ~23 nm that includes the thickness of the three layers (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6A and 6B showing experimental results.

claim: The shape of the crack shows that some VP2 layer has been exposed and its distance to the VP7 layer external face is compatible with the thickness of VP7 and VP6 layers (3.5 and 8 nm, respectively).
source: However, the shape of the crack shows that some VP2 layer has been exposed (Figure 6B, dotted line) and its distance to the VP7 layer external face is compatible with the thickness of VP7 and VP6 layers (3,5 and 8 nm, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B showing experimental results.

claim: Subsequent fatigue cycles after FIC increased the VP2 uncovered area without any signature of the TLP-DLP transition.
source: The subsequent fatigue cycles increased the VP2 uncovered area (Figure 6A#56, Video 6) without any signature of the TLP-DLP transition.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6A and Video 6 showing experimental results.

claim: Combined nanoindentation-fatigue experiments indicate that VP6 hardly survives to VP7 removal, supporting a strong interaction between VP7 and VP6 layers in the presence of Ca.
source: These experiments indicate that VP6 hardly survives to VP7 removal, supporting a strong interaction between VP7 and VP6 layers in the presence of Ca and, once again, a weak binding between VP6 and VP2.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined nanoindentation-fatigue experiment results.

claim: Combined nanoindentation-fatigue experiments indicate a weak binding between VP6 and VP2.
source: These experiments indicate that VP6 hardly survives to VP7 removal, supporting a strong interaction between VP7 and VP6 layers in the presence of Ca and, once again, a weak binding between VP6 and VP2.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined nanoindentation-fatigue experiment results.

claim: The core shell presents a mainly hydrophobic outer surface in agreement with its tendency to form aggregates.
source: Analysis of the electrostatic potential of the different RV particles (Figure 7A–C) shows that the core shell presents a mainly hydrophobic outer surface (Figure 7A) in agreement with its tendency to form aggregates (Labbé et al., 1991; Desselberger et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7A and citations to Labbé et al., 1991; Desselberger et al., 2013.

claim: Treatment of SLP cores with electrolytes or different pH do not solubilize them.
source: While treatment of these cores with electrolytes or different pH do not solubilize them, incubation with some detergents like deoxycholate (Desselberger et al., 2013) or with trehalose (Figure 1E) disperse them and suggest that particle aggregation is produced by hydrophobic forces.
evidence: The claim is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Incubation with some detergents like deoxycholate or with trehalose disperse SLP cores and suggest that particle aggregation is produced by hydrophobic forces.
source: While treatment of these cores with electrolytes or different pH do not solubilize them, incubation with some detergents like deoxycholate (Desselberger et al., 2013) or with trehalose (Figure 1E) disperse them and suggest that particle aggregation is produced by hydrophobic forces.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by a citation to Desselberger et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 1E.

claim: In a RV infection SLP are localized in the viroplasm, where viral RNA packaging and replication occur and where extensive protein-RNA and protein-protein interactions prevent its aggregation.
source: In a RV infection SLP are localized in the viroplasm, where viral RNA packaging and replication occur and where extensive protein-RNA and protein-protein interactions prevent its aggregation (Zeng et al., 1998; Berois et al., 2003; Vende et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zeng et al., 1998; Berois et al., 2003; Vende et al., 2003.

claim: VP6 pear-shaped trimers assemble into five non-equivalent positions to build a T = 13 architecture over the hydrophobic outer surface of the VP2 T = 1 shell.
source: Over the hydrophobic outer surface of the VP2 T = 1 shell, VP6 pear-shaped trimers assemble into five non-equivalent positions (Figure 7D–E, triangles) to build a T = 13 architecture, in what constitutes an extreme example of symmetry mismatch.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7D-E showing structural analysis.

claim: The mismatched interactions between VP6 and VP2 are mainly mediated by the hydrophobic VP6 inward-projecting loop 64–72 that contacts with the SLP outer surface.
source: These mismatched interactions are mainly mediated by the hydrophobic VP6 inward-projecting loop 64–72 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) that contacts with the SLP outer surface, and are not only essential for assembly but also for transcription (Charpilienne et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Charpilienne et al., 2002.

claim: The VP6-VP2 and intertrimeric VP6-VP6 contacts are not only essential for assembly but also for transcription.
source: These mismatched interactions are mainly mediated by the hydrophobic VP6 inward-projecting loop 64–72 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) that contacts with the SLP outer surface, and are not only essential for assembly but also for transcription (Charpilienne et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Charpilienne et al., 2002.

claim: Intertrimeric VP6 contacts are established through their pedestal domains and have local 2-fold contacts.
source: Intertrimeric VP6 contacts are established through their pedestal domains and have local 2-fold contacts.
evidence: The claim is stated as structural knowledge.

claim: Both the VP2-VP6 and the intertrimeric VP6-VP6 contacts are of modest extent.
source: Both the VP2-VP6 and the intertrimeric VP6-VP6 contacts are of modest extent.
evidence: The claim is stated as structural knowledge.

claim: The weak protein-protein interactions described in the structure are in agreement with the experiments showing VP6 trimers are quickly disassembled in fatigue experiments.
source: These weak protein-protein interactions, described in the structure, are in agreement with our experiments. In particular, VP6 trimers are quickly disassembled in fatigue experiments (Figure 5C; blue in Figure 5E), proving poor lateral and perpendicular interactions between VP6 trimers and VP6-VP2 units.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation connecting structural and experimental observations.

claim: The calculation of the electrostatic potential surface of the DLP reveals a very negative outer surface.
source: In contrast with the hydrophobic nature of the SLP outer surface, the calculation of the electrostatic potential surface of the DLP reveals a very negative outer surface (Figure 7B) (Mathieu et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7B and a citation to Mathieu et al., 2001.

claim: The structures of the transcriptionally active particles of other dsRNA viruses present a similar negatively charged outer surface.
source: The structures of the transcriptionally active particles of other dsRNA viruses present a similar negatively charged outer surface (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), which may reflect a common strategy to avoid the interaction with the newly synthesized negative charged transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 2 showing comparative analysis.

claim: The negatively charged outer surface of transcriptionally active dsRNA virus particles may reflect a common strategy to avoid the interaction with the newly synthesized negative charged transcripts.
source: The structures of the transcriptionally active particles of other dsRNA viruses present a similar negatively charged outer surface (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), which may reflect a common strategy to avoid the interaction with the newly synthesized negative charged transcripts.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed electrostatic properties.

claim: VP7 trimers are stabilized through the binding of calcium ions at each subunit interface.
source: VP7 trimers are stabilized through the binding of calcium ions at each subunit interface (Aoki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aoki et al., 2009.

claim: The bottom inner surface of the VP7 trimer has minimal contacts with the VP6 trimer apex of which the most intense is mediated by the VP7 N termini that embraces the underlying VP6 trimer.
source: The bottom inner surface of the VP7 trimer has minimal contacts with the VP6 trimer apex of which the most intense is mediated by the VP7 N termini that embraces the underlying VP6 trimer (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7H showing structural analysis.

claim: VP7 N termini also interact with adjacent VP7 trimers generating a cooperative lattice that reinforce the RV outer shell.
source: These arms also interact with adjacent VP7 trimers generating a cooperative lattice that reinforce the RV outer shell.
evidence: The claim is stated as structural knowledge.

claim: Fatigue experiments demonstrate weak interactions of VP6, both intertrimeric and with the VP2 layer.
source: Our fatigue experiments (Figure 5) demonstrate weak interactions of VP6, both intertrimeric and with the VP2 layer.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the fatigue experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fatigue experiments suggest a strong interaction of the VP7 trimers with the underlying VP6 and with the surrounding VP7 trimers in the presence of calcium.
source: These analyses also suggest a strong interaction of the VP7 trimers with the underlying VP6 and with the surrounding VP7 trimers in the presence of calcium (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the fatigue experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Many viral particles are stabilized by calcium ions bound to the interfaces between their capsomers which is allowed by the unique coordination chemistry of the Ca ion.
source: Many viral particles are stabilized by calcium ions bound to the interfaces between their capsomers which is allowed by the unique coordination chemistry of the Ca ion (Zhou et al., 2009; Carafoli and Krebs, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2009 and Carafoli and Krebs, 2016.

claim: Calcium ions are required to maintain the capsid structural integrity and/or regulate its proper assembly/disassembly.
source: These ions are required to maintain the capsid structural integrity and/or regulate its proper assembly/disassembly (Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2009.

claim: Previous studies have directly probed the mechanical role of calcium ions in the shell stability of tomato bushy stunt virus nanoparticles.
source: Actually, previous studies have directly probed the mechanical role of calcium ions in the shell stability of tomato bushy stunt virus nanoparticles (Llauró et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Llauró et al., 2015.

claim: The inward facing electrostatic potential surface of the VP7 layer is highly negative.
source: Surprisingly, the inward facing electrostatic potential surface of the VP7 layer (Figure 7F) is highly negative.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7F showing electrostatic analysis.

claim: Calcium ions, beyond stabilizing the VP7 trimers, would be sandwiched between the VP7 inner and VP6 outer surfaces to allow their assembly.
source: We propose that calcium ions, beyond stabilizing the VP7 trimers, would be sandwiched between the VP7 inner and VP6 outer surfaces to allow their assembly.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on electrostatic analysis.

claim: VP7 assembles into trimers that are stabilized through the binding of two calcium ions at each subunit interface.
source: VP7 assembles into trimers that are stabilized through the binding of two calcium ions at each subunit interface (Aoki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aoki et al., 2009.

claim: The depletion of calcium will promote the destabilization of the VP7 intertrimeric interactions and induce the rapid disassembly of this shell by the destabilization of the VP7/VP6 electrostatic interactions.
source: Thus, the depletion of calcium will promote the destabilization of the VP7 intertrimeric interactions and induce the rapid disassembly of this shell by the destabilization of the VP7/VP6 electrostatic interactions (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 5B showing experimental results.

claim: The Young's modulus value of the VP7 shell is within the highest values as obtained for bacteriophages.
source: Thus, while the Young's modulus value of the VP7 shell is within the highest values as obtained for bacteriophages (Roos et al., 2012; Ivanovska et al., 2004), the VP6 layer presents the lowest value ever reported for a viral protein shell (Marchetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roos et al., 2012 and Ivanovska et al., 2004.

claim: The VP6 layer presents the lowest Young's modulus value ever reported for a viral protein shell.
source: Thus, while the Young's modulus value of the VP7 shell is within the highest values as obtained for bacteriophages (Roos et al., 2012; Ivanovska et al., 2004), the VP6 layer presents the lowest value ever reported for a viral protein shell (Marchetti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marchetti et al., 2016.

claim: The FE simulations of the TLP show that the stiff VP7 layer accumulates most of the stress during the indentation, protecting the internal VP6 and VP2 layers by shielding the stress transmission to these layers.
source: In fact, the FE simulations of the TLP show that the stiff VP7 layer accumulates most of the stress during the indentation (Figure 4C), protecting the internal VP6 and VP2 layers by shielding the stress transmission to these layers.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the finite element simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Nanoindentation and mechanical fatigue experiments demonstrate that the VP7 shell provides the resistance needed by the RV particle to bear with the severe conditions of extracellular media.
source: Taken together, nanoindentation and mechanical fatigue experiments demonstrate that the VP7 shell provides the resistance needed by the RV particle to bear with the severe conditions of extracellular media.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined nanoindentation and fatigue experiments.

claim: RV is transmitted through the faecal-oral route and has to overcome the stringent physicochemical conditions of digestion at both the stomach and small intestine, where it infects mature enterocytes.
source: RV is transmitted through the faecal-oral route and has to overcome the stringent physicochemical conditions of digestion at both the stomach and small intestine, where it infects mature enterocytes (Estes and Greenberg, 2013; Ramig, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Estes and Greenberg, 2013 and Ramig, 2004.

claim: The viscosity of the chyle is about 10 to 100 times larger than the host cytoplasm and presents higher molecular crowding.
source: The viscosity of the chyle (Jonas, 1976) is about 10 to 100 times larger than the host cytoplasm (Luby-Phelps et al., 1993) and presents higher molecular crowding (Hernando-Pérez et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jonas, 1976; Luby-Phelps et al., 1993; Hernando-Pérez et al., 2014a.

claim: The VP7 shell has to be stable enough to overcome the constant barrage of molecular impacts in the small intestine.
source: Therefore, the VP7 shell has to be stable enough to overcome the constant barrage of molecular impacts in the small intestine.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the environmental conditions RV faces.

claim: Fatigue experiments provide a good approximation for molecular impacts on RV particles.
source: In fact, fatigue experiments provide a good approximation for these molecular impacts on RV particles (Hernando-Pérez et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hernando-Pérez et al., 2014a.

claim: The VP7 shell of TLP is able to withstand fatigue even at 200 pN indicating a strong intercapsomeric linkage.
source: Interestingly, the VP7 shell of TLP is able to withstand fatigue even at 200 pN (Figure 5A) indicating a strong intercapsomeric linkage.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the fatigue experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The labile nature of VP6 layer, showing both the lowest values of elasticity and Young's modulus, is related with their structure (weak contacts of the VP6 trimers with VP2 and between them).
source: The labile nature of VP6 layer, showing both the lowest values of elasticity and Young's modulus, is related with their structure (weak contacts of the VP6 trimers with VP2 and between them) and we propose that this feature is necessary for its function.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation connecting mechanical properties to structure.

claim: The labile nature of VP6 layer is necessary for its function.
source: The labile nature of VP6 layer, showing both the lowest values of elasticity and Young's modulus, is related with their structure (weak contacts of the VP6 trimers with VP2 and between them) and we propose that this feature is necessary for its function.
evidence: The claim is a proposed functional interpretation.

claim: It has been suggested that removal of VP7 causes the dilation of the particle pentameric channels allowing the flux of nucleotides, ions and transcripts.
source: It has been suggested that removal of VP7 causes the dilation of the particle pentameric channels allowing the flux of nucleotides, ions and transcripts (Chen et al., 2009; Aiyegbo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009 and Aiyegbo et al., 2013.

claim: The removal of VP7 promotes the outward movement of the VP6 pentameric trimers.
source: The removal of VP7 promotes the outward movement of the VP6 pentameric trimers.
evidence: The claim is stated as a known structural change.

claim: The conformational change in VP6 is transmitted through the underlying VP2 decamer to the VP1 polymerase, enabling its activity.
source: This conformational change is transmitted through the underlying VP2 decamer to the VP1 polymerase, enabling its activity.
evidence: The claim is stated as a known mechanism.

claim: In MVM, a similar conformational dynamics is favored by a low mechanical stability.
source: In other viruses, such as MVM (Castellanos et al., 2012) a similar conformational dynamics is favored by a low mechanical stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Castellanos et al., 2012.

claim: The increase of local stiffness in MVM mutants blocks the conformational changes required for dsDNA translocation.
source: In particular, the increase of local stiffness in MVM mutants blocks the conformational changes required for dsDNA translocation.
evidence: The claim is stated as a known result from MVM studies.

claim: The high flexibility resulting from the low mechanical stability of the trimeric VP6 layer would favor its functional roles.
source: Similarly, the high flexibility resulting from the low mechanical stability of the trimeric VP6 layer would favor its functional roles: this thick layer becomes the adaptor that allows the transformation of a highly hydrophobic SLP into a negative-charged DLP, overcoming the symmetry mismatch between the T = 1 and T = 13 layers, and generating a transcriptionally active particle.
evidence: The claim is a proposed functional interpretation.

claim: The VP6 shell constitutes the thickest and, according to the data, the softest layer of the RV particle, which allows for large deformations when TLP or DLP are adsorbed.
source: The VP6 shell constitutes the thickest and, according to our data, the softest layer of the RV particle, which allows for large deformations when TLP or DLP are adsorbed (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SLP exists only in the viroplasm environment during RNA packaging and replication.
source: Finally, the SLP exists only in the viroplasm environment during RNA packaging and replication.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about SLP localization.

claim: The high electrodensity of the viroplasm is a signature of a large concentration of macromolecules that results in a higher molecular crowding than the cytoplasm.
source: The high electrodensity of the viroplasm is a signature of a large concentration of macromolecules that results in a higher molecular crowding than the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about viroplasm properties.

claim: The higher molecular crowding in the viroplasm would explain the higher Young's modulus value of VP2 layer when compared with that of VP6.
source: This fact would explain the higher Young's modulus value of VP2 layer when compared with that of VP6.
evidence: The claim is a proposed explanation connecting environment to mechanical properties.

claim: The Young's modulus of VP2 combined with a presumably smaller adsorption energy with the substrate, result in non-deformed particle after adsorption.
source: This Young's modulus combined with a presumably smaller adsorption energy with the substrate, result in non-deformed particle after adsorption, as it happens with other virus capsids (Carrasco et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by a citation to Carrasco et al., 2009.

claim: The biophysical properties and interactions of the three particle shells are finely tuned to produce an infective RV virion.
source: In this mechanical study of a multi-layered virus we have shown how the biophysical properties and interactions of the three particle shells are finely tuned to produce an infective RV virion.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The high mechanical strength provided by the strong VP7-VP7 and VP7-VP6 interactions relates to protection tasks.
source: While the high mechanical strength provided by the strong VP7-VP7 and VP7-VP6 interactions (Figure 7H, black springs) relates to protection tasks, the lower resistance of the VP6-VP6 and VP6-VP2 interactions (Figure 7H, white springs) guarantees the conformational dynamics required for transcription.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 7H.

claim: The lower resistance of the VP6-VP6 and VP6-VP2 interactions guarantees the conformational dynamics required for transcription.
source: While the high mechanical strength provided by the strong VP7-VP7 and VP7-VP6 interactions (Figure 7H, black springs) relates to protection tasks, the lower resistance of the VP6-VP6 and VP6-VP2 interactions (Figure 7H, white springs) guarantees the conformational dynamics required for transcription.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by reference to Figure 7H.

claim: The interference with the finely tuned mechanical regulation offers new venues for development of antiviral strategies.
source: Importantly, the interference with this finely tuned mechanical regulation offers new venues for development of antiviral strategies.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal for future applications.
